title: Fair4All Finance Report Flags Uneven Access for 16.8m Disabled Consumers
snippet: A Fair4All Finance and PwC report finds UK financial services failing disabled consumers through inconsistent underwriting, digital barriers and a structural gap in The post Fair4All Finance Report Flags Uneven Access for 16.8m Disabled Consumers appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
A new report from financial inclusion body Fair4All Finance, authored with PwC, has found that UK financial services consistently produce uneven outcomes for the country’s 16.8 million disabled consumers. The study, titled “Beyond Uneven Terrain: improving the disability landscape in financial services”, draws on reviews of 29 providers, 30 stakeholder interviews and a survey of 102 disabled consumers, and identifies structural failures rather than isolated failures of goodwill.

The researchers estimate that disabled people hold approximately £274 billion in annual spending power, and that a more inclusive financial services market could generate at least £6.4 billion in additional annual economic output. The headline number signals this is not purely a social argument: it is a commercial one.

Three structural failures

The report groups its findings around three interlocking problems.

The first is what researchers call the “missing middle” in supported access. Many disabled consumers who need help managing their finances face a binary choice: act entirely independently, or hand over control through a formal legal instrument such as a lasting power of attorney. The gap between those two options is largely unfilled, which has pushed some individuals toward informal workarounds such as sharing debit cards, PINs or passwords with carers. These workarounds expose consumers to fraud risk and leave providers without visibility of what is happening in an account.

The second concerns digital access. Of the 29 providers reviewed, 23 maintained dedicated accessibility pages or hubs, but only nine demonstrated highly visible evidence of testing or co-design with disabled people, and only seven addressed disability or accessibility in their public reporting. Two-factor authentication, verification workflows and periodic app redesigns were all identified as sources of disruption for consumers using assistive technologies.

The third area covers product decisioning and underwriting. The report found that automated models can make inaccurate assumptions about disabled applicants, producing declines or inflated premiums that the individual has no straightforward mechanism to challenge. Benefit income is treated inconsistently across mortgage affordability assessments: some lenders accept disability-related payments towards affordability calculations; others exclude or deduct them without explanation. One interviewee described being classified as “uninsurable” and said the experience made them feel “as if you’re a leper.”

Regulatory and commercial read-across

Kate Pender, CEO of Fair4All Finance

The findings arrive in a regulatory environment that is pushing financial services firms toward evidenced, not aspirational, inclusion. The FCA‘s Consumer Duty, in force since July 2023, requires firms to demonstrate good outcomes for all retail customers, including those with characteristics of vulnerability. The Duty puts the burden of proof on providers rather than consumers, and disability sits squarely within the vulnerability definitions the regulator uses. Firms that cannot show outcome monitoring across disabled customer segments face increasing supervisory risk.

Fair4All Finance’s chief executive, Kate Pender, made the commercial case plainly: “Designing an inclusive financial system is not just a social obligation, it is an untapped commercial opportunity that could deliver at least an additional £6.4bn annual boost to the UK economy.”

The report recommends expanding the voluntary Disability Finance Code into retail financial services, piloting supported access mechanisms that protect against fraud without removing consumer autonomy, embedding lived experience in product development governance, and reviewing how automated decisioning and benefit income treatment affect disabled applicants for credit and insurance.

Howard Taylor, director at PwC UK, noted the compound pressures: “Disabled people frequently face higher day-to-day costs and lower average incomes, contributing to lower financial resilience, while also encountering barriers when accessing the products, services and support they need.”

The push to extend the Disability Finance Code across retail financial services is the policy lever worth watching. If adopted at industry scale, it would shift accessibility from a discretionary practice to a defined standard, with implications for product design, underwriting governance and digital channel investment across the sector.

title: Why Stablecoin Yield Is the Next Regulatory Flashpoint
snippet: Trace Finance CEO Bernardo Brites argues that yield, not issuance, is where stablecoin regulation gets hard, and that products must show who owes the customer. The post Why Stablecoin Yield Is the Next Regulatory Flashpoint appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Stablecoin rules have started to cover reserves and redemption. The harder policy question is what happens when a payment token begins to offer its holder a return, and which regulator that return belongs to.

Bernardo Brites, co-founder and CEO at Trace Finance

Bernardo Brites is co-founder and CEO of Trace Finance, a regulated banking correspondent that connects stablecoin settlement to local banking systems in Brazil, the United States and emerging markets. In this opinion piece he argues that yield products need to be separated clearly from the payment tokens they are built around. Trace Finance operates on regulated, bank-connected payment infrastructure and may benefit from the policy direction discussed. The views are his own.

Stablecoins have moved beyond a debate about issuance. Policymakers face a harder task. They must separate the payment token from the financial product built around it. A token that redeems at par and holds liquid reserves presents one set of risks. A product that pays a holder for keeping that token presents another.

That separation will shape the next phase of stablecoin regulation. A yield feature can be deposit-taking, lending, a securities offering, or a reward programme, depending on how it works. The label on the token tells a little about the regulator. The legal and economic design of the return matters more.

The payment token has a clearer rulebook

The US GENIUS Act gave stablecoin issuers a clear starting point. The law requires permitted issuers to maintain identifiable reserves at least equal to outstanding payment stablecoins. It also bars an issuer from paying interest or yield merely because a person holds its token. Those rules address two direct questions. Can the holder redeem, and what assets support that redemption?

The next question is less settled. The Act does not expressly settle every arrangement in which an affiliate, platform, lender, or other third party pays a return connected to a stablecoin. The White House has described this as a gap that can let firms offer interest-bearing arrangements outside the issuer itself. That distinction will attract close attention because the economic result for a customer can resemble issuer-paid yield even when the legal structure differs.

Yield is a product category, not a single feature

The term ‘stablecoin yield’ hides important differences. A customer can lend tokens to a platform that lends them onward. A platform can place reserves or customer assets in short-term instruments and share some return. A firm can pay a reward from its own balance sheet to encourage payment activity. A customer can also use a token as collateral and receive a return through a separate investment product.

These models create distinct claims on assets, loss paths, and duties to the customer. Regulators should ask who promises the return, where the funds sit, who controls the assets, and who carries losses when a borrower fails or a market moves. They should also ask if a customer can redeem the payment token at par while the yield product remains open or suffers a loss.

The US Securities and Exchange Commission’s Division of Corporation Finance said in April 2025 that its statement on certain reserve-backed payment stablecoins did not express a view on yield-bearing stablecoins. It said the legal analysis depends on the facts of a particular stablecoin and the circumstances of its offer and sale. This position is not a final rule, but it makes the boundary plain. The payment-token analysis does not settle the legal treatment of the return built around it.

Banking links make the boundaries testable

The strongest products will make their boundaries visible. A payment stablecoin should have clear reserve, redemption, and disclosure terms. A yield product should state its funding source, its counterparty, its loss rules, and the legal claim a customer receives. The two products may work together, but they should not depend on customer confusion about where payment funds end and investment risk begins.

Bank-connected infrastructure can support this separation because authorised financial institutions already operate with account records, customer checks, payment controls, and defined responsibility for funds. The value is not a bank logo on a token. The value is an operating structure that can show which party holds the funds, which party owes the customer, and which rules apply when a transaction fails.

Brazil offers a useful operational example. Banco Central do Brasil‘s Resolution BCB 520 places virtual asset service providers within a defined regulatory perimeter and sets rules for their activity. It does not provide a final answer to the classification of every yield product. It shows why regulated local settlement and clear responsibility matter when stablecoins move between token networks and national payment systems.

The test comes during stress

Some people will argue that strict limits on stablecoin yield will push customers to offshore platforms or unregulated protocols. That risk is real. A rule that blocks every return product could reduce choice and move activity into structures that give users less information.

The answer is not to treat every payment token and every yield product as the same thing. Regulators can permit products that explain their funding, reserve treatment, redemption rights, fees, and loss allocation. They can set different rules for a payment balance, a lending account, and an investment product. That approach gives firms room to compete on product design while giving customers a way to judge the risk they accept.

Stablecoin issuance is becoming a question of reserves, licensing, and redemption. Stablecoin yield is becoming a question of control, funding, loss, and disclosure. The firms that can answer those questions in plain terms will have a stronger basis for operating as enforcement and rulemaking develop.

title: Furaha Reaches 100,000 Ugandan Children with School-Fee Credit
snippet: The SC Ventures-incubated lender now targets 10 million children across Africa by 2030, using alternative data to unlock bank credit for parents. The post Furaha Reaches 100,000 Ugandan Children with School-Fee Credit appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Furaha Financial, an education lending fintech incubated by SC Ventures and headquartered in Kampala, says it has helped parents finance school fees for 100,000 Ugandan children since launching in 2024. The company is now setting its sights on 10 million children across Africa by 2030, positioning the Uganda milestone as a proof of concept for a broader continental rollout.

Yustus Aribariho, co-founder at Furaha Financial

The model is built around a structural mismatch in African household finance: school-fee payment deadlines rarely align with the irregular income cycles of informal workers, and millions of parents lack the payslips, collateral or formal credit histories that commercial banks conventionally require. Furaha sits between these parents and its banking partners, namely Diamond Trust Bank Uganda, Cairo Bank Uganda, Opportunity Bank and FINCA Uganda, providing the technology layer for customer onboarding, KYC, alternative-data credit scoring, loan disbursement and collections.

“Millions of parents have never been seen by traditional credit systems, not necessarily because they can’t repay, but because the data needed to assess them has not existed in one place,” said Yustus Aribariho, co-founder of Furaha. “By bringing together mobile-money, school-payment and other alternative data, we can give financial institutions a broader view of customers.”

The ecosystem model

Ian Fernandes, co-founder at Furaha Financial

Furaha’s approach is deliberately multi-sided. Beyond its bank partners, the platform connects mobile-money operators MTN and Airtel with school-fee payment platforms SchoolPay, SurePay and PegPay. Co-founder Ian Fernandes described the rationale as recognising that no single institution could independently solve the problem each term, and that Furaha’s role is to act as the connective layer across the ecosystem.

Chief executive Dennis Musinguzi described the 100,000 figure as a proof point rather than a destination, and said the next phase involves taking the model to more families and more African countries. The company has not yet disclosed which markets it intends to enter next, nor detailed the funding position that will support that expansion.

Market context and regulatory landscape

The education-finance segment remains largely untapped by formal lenders across sub-Saharan Africa, where UNESCO estimates that the region accounts for nearly 40 per cent of the world’s out-of-school children. UNESCO’s 2026 Global Education Monitoring Report notes that enrolment across the region has expanded, yet the absolute number of out-of-school children continues to rise, partly because financing is only one of several barriers to attendance.

Furaha’s claim to be the first lending fintech in Africa to channel affordable commercial-bank financing specifically toward education needs is notable but not independently verified. The broader alternative-data credit scoring space is active across East and West Africa, with several fintechs, including M-Kopa, Tala and branch-network lenders, using mobile and transaction data to extend consumer credit. What distinguishes Furaha is the specific school-fee use case and the direct integration with fee-payment platforms, which creates a closed-loop data environment that may improve repayment predictability.

From a regulatory standpoint, Furaha operates as a technology platform rather than a licensed lender itself, meaning credit risk sits with its partner banks. This structure is common in embedded-finance and banking-as-a-service arrangements globally and allows faster scaling without the capital and prudential requirements of a full banking licence. However, it places Furaha in a similar position to the bank-fintech middle-layer models that have attracted regulatory scrutiny in more developed markets: the platform’s operational resilience and data-governance practices become critical to its banking partners’ own compliance posture.

The next milestones to watch are geographic expansion announcements, any disclosed funding round to support the 2030 ambition, and whether Furaha extends its bank partnership roster beyond Uganda.

title: Detect It, Then Stop It: Inside the First VerityX Labs Challenge for UAE Banks
snippet: VerityX Innovation Labs has launched a UAE challenge seeking AI solutions that detect and stop mule-account fraud in real time, with a focus on accuracy, explainability and bank-ready deployment. Do you like this personality? The post Detect It, Then Stop It: Inside the First VerityX Labs Challenge for UAE Banks appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
A fraud score is not a defence. That, in a sentence, is the premise of the first challenge to run through VerityX Innovation Labs, the Emirates Institute of Finance-backed programme that aims to compress the UAE’s bank innovation cycle from twelve months to ninety days. The brief, AI-Powered Mule Account Detection and Interdiction for UAE Banks, asks fintechs for something the market has been slow to supply: a system that spots a money mule early and then does something about it, inside controls a bank can actually operate and defend to its regulator.

The target is a hard one precisely because it looks ordinary. Mule accounts are the settlement layer of almost every consumer fraud and laundering scheme running in the UAE. Victims of investment, romance, job and impersonation scams are directed to move funds into accounts controlled, knowingly or otherwise, by third parties, who then layer the money rapidly across banks, wallets and borders. The account itself is legitimate and KYC-verified, behaving in a subtly abnormal way, which is why rules-based monitoring routinely misses it until the money has gone. The brief notes that more than half of UAE residents report being targeted by a financial fraud attempt every month, with bank transfers and cards the most-targeted channels, and that mules are recruited continuously through fake job offers and social media, so the population of at-risk accounts refreshes faster than any blocklist can track it.

Regulation supplies the deadline. CBUAE Notice No. CBUAE/FCMCP/2025/3057 makes mule-account detection an explicit supervisory expectation, requiring licensed institutions to identify mule accounts early on the basis of unexpected or suspicious transaction patterns, to run real-time transaction monitoring around the clock with per-transaction risk scoring, and to stop or decline suspicious activity as it happens. Most of those requirements carried a compliance deadline of 31 March 2026, with penalties of up to AED 250,000 per violation. The supervisory expectation is therefore already live, and the gap between what banks are required to do and what their current stacks can do is what the challenge is designed to close.

The brief splits the problem in two. On detection, it asks entrants to surface accounts receiving and moving illicit funds before or as the money moves, using signals including rapid in-and-out flows, fan-in and fan-out patterns, pass-through balances that hover near zero, sudden divergence from an account’s own behavioural baseline across velocity, counterparties, channels, devices and geography, network links to already-suspected mules through shared devices and coordinated timing, and the tell-tale profile of newly recruited or dormant-then-active accounts showing signs of remote control.

The second half is where the brief departs from a conventional fraud tender. Detection must convert into what VerityX calls action to stop: a proportionate, timely intervention that halts loss without punishing legitimate customers. That means real-time hold, decline or step-up on outbound transactions from a suspected mule, prioritised and explainable alerts with the evidence behind each decision attached for fraud and AML investigators, a feedback loop so investigator outcomes retrain the model and drive false positives down, and support for inter-bank signal sharing where funds move across institutions, within legal and data-protection limits.

Entrants build and test inside the VerityX Labs Sandbox rather than against a slide deck. Participating fintechs get synthetic and anonymised UAE-representative transaction, account and device datasets seeded with mule typologies and labelled outcomes; an isolated environment for running detection models and interdiction logic against streaming and batch data without touching live customer systems; reference API patterns and event schemas that mirror how a sponsor bank’s core, payments and case-management systems would call the solution; a common evaluation harness with holdout scenarios so every entrant is scored on the same basis; and structured sessions with fraud, AML, data and regulatory specialists.

Scoring reflects the brief’s central argument that deployability is as decisive as accuracy. Detection performance, covering precision, recall, speed and the false-positive burden on genuine customers, carries 30 per cent. Action and interdiction, judged on the effectiveness, proportionality and safety of the stop mechanism and on measurable loss prevented, carries 25 per cent. Explainability and auditability, meaning clear per-decision reasoning a bank can defend to CBUAE and to its own customers, carries 20 per cent. Deployability, covering latency, scalability, integration effort and fit with existing bank controls, carries 15 per cent, and compliance and data ethics the remaining 10 per cent. A solution that detects brilliantly but cannot be run inside a UAE bank’s control environment will not win.

The programme is looking for fintechs and regtechs with working capability in fraud detection, transaction monitoring, behavioural analytics, graph and network analysis, or AI and machine learning for financial crime, able to deploy and iterate within the sandbox timeframe and to integrate by API. A UAE presence or licence is helpful but not required, and the brief explicitly welcomes early-stage teams with a strong, novel approach. The indicative timeline runs two weeks to register, one to accredit, two to build and test, and one to evaluate in front of sponsor banks and regulator observers, with selected solutions progressing to a controlled pilot with a sponsor bank.

That last phase is the point of the whole exercise. The Innovation Labs model exists to give the UAE’s banks a governed route from proof of value to production pilot without the multi-month procurement cycle that kills most bank-fintech pilots before they start, and the mule challenge is the first test of whether it works. Fintechs and regtechs wanting to take part can register at the VerityX Labs platform, referencing the Mule Account Detection Challenge, and complete accreditation to gain access.

title: OakNorth Enters Children’s Savings with 3.5% Junior Cash ISA
snippet: OakNorth has launched its first Junior Cash ISA at 3.5% AER, partnering with childcare app Bubble to target the 85% of UK children without The post OakNorth Enters Children’s Savings with 3.5% Junior Cash ISA appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
OakNorth Bank has launched its first Junior Cash ISA (JISA), carrying a 3.5% AER rate and marking the digital bank’s first product designed for under-18s in its 11-year history. The account opens from £1, accepts transfers from existing JISAs held elsewhere without affecting the annual allowance, and is available to children aged 14 and under at launch. Deposits are locked until the child turns 18, with FSCS protection up to £120,000.

The bank, which says it holds more than £7bn in deposits from around 250,000 adult savers, is framing the JISA as a natural extension of an established savings franchise rather than a diversification into unfamiliar territory. OakNorth already offers an Easy Access Cash ISA and a Fixed Rate Cash ISA to adult customers, so the infrastructure and regulatory permissions were largely in place. The product can be opened and managed entirely through the OakNorth app or online, with an account-opening time the bank puts at under ten minutes.

The Bubble tie-up

Thomas Robinson, product director at OakNorth

Alongside the product launch, OakNorth has struck a partnership with Bubble, a UK childcare app, offering customers who open a JISA two free hours of babysitting through the platform. Tom Mursell, head of growth at Bubble, described alignment between the two companies’ missions: making childcare and finance more accessible to UK families. The incentive is modest in cash terms, but its logic is clear: the target customer is a working parent with limited time, and a practical, immediate benefit sits more comfortably with that audience than a rate comparison alone.

OakNorth said it is also exploring deeper ties with businesses from its own lending portfolio, which includes nursery groups Storal, Kinderzimmer and ICP Educare, as well as family retailer Mamas & Papas. If those relationships are formalised, the bank could position itself as an embedded financial partner within the broader childcare and family-spending ecosystem, a more defensible distribution moat than rate alone.

Thomas Robinson, product director at OakNorth, pointed to a significant market gap: “85% of young people in the UK don’t currently have a JISA, so there’s huge, untapped potential here.”

Market context

The Junior ISA market in the UK has historically been dominated by established wealth managers, building societies and large retail banks offering stocks-and-shares as well as cash versions of the wrapper. The current JISA annual subscription limit sits at £9,000 per tax year, shared across cash and stocks-and-shares accounts. At 3.5% AER, OakNorth’s rate is competitive in the cash segment, though rates in this market have been adjusting as the Bank of England’s rate cycle turns. Providers including Coventry Building Society and Nationwide have also been active in this segment, and any easing cycle will put pressure on variable-rate cash JISAs across the board.

The regulatory backdrop is straightforward. OakNorth is authorised by the Prudential Regulation Authority and regulated by the FCA, and the JISA is a well-established, HMRC-administered product with no novel compliance risk attached. The FSCS cover ceiling of £120,000 per child is notably higher than the standard £85,000 adult deposit limit, a detail the bank has chosen to lead with as a trust signal for parents depositing over longer horizons.

The near-term test for OakNorth is whether the Bubble partnership and potential nursery-network distribution channels meaningfully accelerate JISA take-up beyond what a rate-competitive product alone would achieve. If the lending-portfolio partnerships are converted into live distribution deals, the bank will have built a family-finance corridor that is harder for a rate-matching competitor to replicate quickly.

title: How agentic payments present risk
snippet: “There's no clear legal rule for who bears the loss when an AI tool exceeds its mandate,” writes one financial services consultant. “That's a problem for issuers as they contemplate making credentials available to AI tools.”
fullText:
Aaron Cheiffetz is an analyst and executive strategist in the financial services industry, working with banking leaders on artificial intelligence governance, enterprise architecture, regulatory compliance and operational resiliency. He is based in Charlotte, North Carolina.

In the debit-card context, Regulation E generally limits a consumer's liability for unauthorized transfers involving a lost or stolen debit card to $50 if the loss is reported within two business days. But Regulation E excludes from its definition of an “unauthorized electronic fund transfer” a transfer initiated by a person to whom the consumer furnished the access device, unless the consumer has notified the financial institution that transfers by that person are no longer authorized. 

The official commentary goes further: if a consumer furnishes an access device and grants another person authority to make transfers, the consumer can remain liable even when that person exceeds the authority given. Regulation E defines "person" to include both natural persons and organizations, including corporations. 

Optional Caption

Permission granted by Aaron Cheiffetz

What it doesn't say is how that rule applies when credentials are furnished to software operated by a company. A January research report by the Consumer Bankers Association asks whether sharing credentials with an AI tool could trigger this exclusion and leave the consumer responsible for the agent's mistakes.

In the credit-card context, the Truth in Lending Act, implemented by Regulation Z, provides a similar unauthorized-use framework that turns on whether another person had actual, implied, or apparent authority to use the account. Here too, it's unclear how that rule applies when an AI tool acts on a cardholder's behalf.

Visa and Mastercard have zero-liability policies for unauthorized transactions that go beyond federal law. But those policies still depend on a transaction being classified as unauthorized. They don't clearly resolve what happens when a consumer authorized an agent to transact but disputes whether a particular purchase fell within the scope of that authority. 

These are the kinds of issues that should be addressed in agentic payment frameworks, which Mastercard and Visa are developing. Such frameworks envision the payment system recording or validating instructions given by users to agents and taking steps to make sure agents and merchants are who they purport to be and that transactions remain consistent with the consumer's mandate. 

But a host of questions remain. There's no clear legal rule for who bears the loss when an AI tool exceeds its mandate. That's a problem for issuers as they contemplate making credentials available to AI tools. 

Where risks aren't adequately addressed and priced, issuers may be tempted to act defensively by agreeing to credential-sharing only with sophisticated AI-tool providers under negotiated contracts, adopting onerous identity-confirmation processes, or refusing transactions in some circumstances. All of this would tilt the playing field in favor of incumbent platforms.

Some clarity about liability for unauthorized transactions will be important before agentic payments are rolled out more broadly. Voluntary efforts by banks and payment networks won't go far enough to assuage concerns. More fundamental issues of consumer liability need to be addressed. 

At minimum, three things need to happen. 

First, laws should distinguish between a consumer’s own acts and the acts of others, including AI tools acting on a consumer's behalf. Second, when consumers give others authority to initiate financial transactions, the parameters of that authority, such as amounts, merchants, timing, and other limits, should be documented in a form the payment system can use. Third, the allocation of losses among issuers, payment networks, merchants, and AI-tool providers should not be an issue for consumers.

title: S&P Global Ratings Launches Vault Risk Assessment for Onchain Lending
snippet: S&P Global Ratings has introduced a six-factor analytical framework to assess risk in digital asset lending vaults, a market that has grown to The post S&P Global Ratings Launches Vault Risk Assessment for Onchain Lending appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
S&P Global Ratings has launched its Vault Risk Assessment (VRA), a new analytical framework designed to give institutional investors an independent, forward-looking view of risk in digital asset lending vaults. The product is not a credit rating; instead, it delivers a letter-based opinion across six risk factors: portfolio credit quality, liquidity mismatch, curator risk, blockchain risk, protocol risk, and vault security and governance.

The timing is notable. Total deposits in digital asset lending vaults reached approximately $10 billion as of September 2026, up from $1.5 billion two years earlier. That sevenfold expansion has attracted institutional capital that requires a risk governance framework before it can be deployed at scale, and S&P is positioning the VRA to fill that gap.

What vaults are, and why they need independent assessment

Yann Le Pallec, president of S&P Global Ratings

Digital asset lending vaults pool investor deposits on a blockchain and deploy them according to defined strategies, functioning much like managed fixed income funds. Positions can be executed entirely through smart contracts or managed discretionarily by human curators. Depositors receive share tokens representing their proportional claim on the vault’s assets.

Despite the on-chain transparency that blockchain infrastructure provides, strategy and risk disclosures for individual vaults have typically been limited. Point-in-time transparency around transactions does not tell an investor whether a curator is over-concentrated, whether the underlying protocol has been audited, or whether redemption liquidity matches the deposit base. The VRA is designed to address that structural opacity.

Yann Le Pallec, president of S&P Global Ratings, said the firm’s commitment to analytical rigour extends to rapidly growing digital markets. “The Vault Risk Assessment will empower investors and foster greater confidence and stability as capital flows into these new digital structures.” James Wiemken, Executive Managing Director and Head of Global Ratings Services, described varying disclosure standards in the vault market as creating “a clear need for a standardised, independent risk perspective.”

S&P Global Ratings said it will publish initial VRAs in future announcements; no specific vault has been assessed under the framework yet.

A broader digital assets strategy at S&P Global

The VRA launch is the latest in a series of moves by S&P Global to extend its analytical infrastructure into onchain finance. In September 2026, the company announced an agreement to acquire OpenZeppelin, a widely used smart contract security standard, and led a strategic investment in Kaiko, the digital asset market data provider. S&P Global Ratings has also issued what it describes as the first credit rating of a DeFi protocol, applied to Sky Protocol, and the first structured finance rating backed by bitcoin, for a product known as Ledn.

Taken together, the acquisitions and product launches suggest S&P Global is pursuing a systematic rather than opportunistic entry into digital assets, building data infrastructure via Kaiko, security standards via OpenZeppelin, and analytical products across stablecoins, DeFi protocols and now vaults.

Regulatory and competitive context

For institutional investors, independent risk assessment frameworks for onchain vehicles are increasingly important as regulators in the EU, UK and US move to define how digital asset funds should be treated for capital and custody purposes. MiCA, which became fully effective across EU member states in 2025, sets out requirements for crypto-asset service providers but does not yet offer a complete framework for onchain pooled vehicles of the vault type. A recognised third-party assessment standard could become a compliance input rather than merely a voluntary due diligence tool.

In the broader market, other ratings agencies and data providers have taken cautious or incremental positions on DeFi risk. S&P Global’s willingness to publish framework-level opinions on vault risk, backed by named acquisition activity and a defined six-factor model, represents a more committed infrastructure play than most peers have attempted. Whether the VRA becomes a market standard or remains one input among many will depend on how quickly institutions adopt it and whether regulators reference it in guidance.

title: Salad’s Alex Marsh on Lending Beyond the Credit Score
snippet: Salad group CEO and former Klarna UK chief Alex Marsh on why Open Banking data, not credit scores, should decide who in the UK can borrow affordably. The post Salad’s Alex Marsh on Lending Beyond the Credit Score appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Salad puts the number of UK consumers labelled underserved or too risky for mainstream credit at more than 20 million. The lender, which describes itself as the UK’s largest consumer lending Community Development Finance Institution (CDFI), assesses those borrowers using Open Banking transaction data rather than credit scores.

Alex Marsh, Group CEO of Salad

Its group CEO, Alex Marsh, was previously UK CEO of Klarna. He joined Salad in 2023 as a non-executive director and chaired the Salad Finance board before stepping up to lead the group. Speaking to The Fintech Times, he set out what transaction data shows that a credit file does not, and what it would take for mainstream lenders to serve the borrowers they currently turn away.

Marsh’s starting point is that a credit score looks backwards. “A credit score can tell you a lot about someone’s past if they’ve used credit products, but very little about how they are managing their money today,” he said. “It can capture missed payments or a CCJ that may sit on someone’s file for years, but it often will not tell you whether they are paying their rent on time, covering their bills, managing a tight budget well or showing signs of financial stress right now.”

Open Banking, he argued, fills that gap with a real-time picture of income, expenditure and financial behaviour. “Having analysed billions of transactions at Salad, what we see again and again is that many people who are declined by mainstream lenders are actually managing their finances responsibly, living within their monthly paycheck and meeting all their payments such as direct debits,” he said.

“They are not necessarily shut out because they cannot manage their money. Often, they manage it much better than people who have a larger income. They are shut out because the traditional credit score system does not have enough information to understand them properly.”

The price of being declined

For many of Salad’s customers the realistic alternatives are narrow. Marsh said they can include “high-cost short-term credit, doorstep lending and, at the worst end of the market, unregulated lenders.” Salad says its customers save an average of £454 on a typical £1,075 loan compared with the lenders otherwise available to them.

“The £454 average saving matters because it is not simply about offering a cheaper loan,” Marsh said. “For someone managing a tight household budget, that difference can determine whether borrowing remains affordable or becomes something they struggle to get out of.”

In his view, mainstream lenders either decline this group or do not compete for it, often because traditional credit data suggests more risk than a fuller picture of current finances supports. “The result is a real contradiction: people with the least financial headroom can end up paying the highest price for credit,” he said.

A market failure, not a niche

Marsh frames the gap as a commercial problem as much as a social one. He pointed to around £2bn of unmet credit demand in the UK, and to an estimate from Fair4All Finance that improving financial inclusion could add roughly £7bn a year to the economy. “So this is not just a social issue; it is a significant market failure and a commercial opportunity,” he said.

Most of the tools needed already exist, he argued. Open Banking gives lenders a clearer view of current affordability and removes the need for manual underwriting, which at some lenders still means applicants sending in scans of bank statements and payslips. “The other big barrier is appetite: too many lenders still see this segment as either too risky or too expensive to serve,” he said.

Salad received more than one million applications last year and has lent over £300m to more than 190,000 customers since it launched in 2018. “That is not a niche market or a charitable exercise,” Marsh said. “It is a sizeable group of consumers with genuine demand.” Regulation could speed the shift by supporting affordability-led lending and better use of Open Banking, he added, but in the end the decision sits with lenders, who he said “need to stop asking whether this market is worth serving and start asking how to serve it responsibly.”

What Klarna taught him

Marsh’s time at Klarna shaped his view that lending at scale is a data problem. “What Klarna taught me is that offering consumer credit at scale, and importantly with sustainable unit economics, is fundamentally a data challenge,” he said. “It is critical that you make good lending decisions for the customer and the lender, using the best possible information.”

What he had to unlearn, he said, was “the assumption that the traditional credit system has already solved this for all consumers. It hasn’t, and particularly for consumers on lower incomes or those with a limited recent credit history.” People often come to Salad at a pressing moment: to fix a car, replace an essential appliance or deal with an unexpected bill.

“We are not arguing that everyone should have access to credit,” he said. “We are arguing that everyone should have the opportunity to be assessed fairly.”

Avoiding a new black box

Richer data raises its own question: whether one opaque score is simply being swapped for another. Marsh said a decline at Salad should be “rooted in affordability rather than a historic marker on a credit file”, and that where possible the lender should be able to explain what is driving the decision “in terms a customer can actually understand”.

Salad says it was the first lender to embed benefit checking into its application journey, so that an application can still help someone identify support they may be entitled to when the company cannot lend. “Ultimately, using better data only works if it leads to better decisions and greater transparency,” Marsh said. “The aim is not to create a more sophisticated black box; it is to understand someone’s circumstances more accurately and lend only where we believe it is genuinely affordable.”

The next two years

Marsh is blunt about the pace of change in credit. “Today you can open a bank account in minutes or move money across borders in seconds, but the technology used to determine whether you’re safe to lend to was built for a different era,” he said. “Technology simply hasn’t caught up and the people on the edges have paid the price.”

The shift he wants is for Open Banking to become the normal way affordability is assessed, rather than a bolt-on. Salad says the benefit checks built into its applications have flagged £872m in unclaimed benefits for more than 300,000 of its applicants, and it reports every repayment to the major credit agencies as part of a credit rehabilitation offer intended to give borrowers a route back into mainstream credit.

Marsh called two years an ambitious timeline for Open Banking-based lending to become the norm for underserved borrowers. “It’s on the market to recognise both the societal need and commercial opportunity, and act,” he said.

title: Fipto and Spiko Link Atablecoin Rails to UCITS T-Bill Funds
snippet: The Paris-based partnership lets corporate treasurers allocate idle EURC and USDC balances into regulated UCITS money market funds without leaving Fipto's platform. The post Fipto and Spiko Link Atablecoin Rails to UCITS T-Bill Funds appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Fipto, the stablecoin-powered B2B payments and treasury platform, has partnered with Spiko Finance SAS to give corporate clients a route from idle stablecoin balances into regulated UCITS money market funds. The arrangement, announced on 5 October 2026, is designed to close the gap between round-the-clock stablecoin settlement and the weekday-only availability of traditional cash management products.

The deal

Patrick Mollard, CEO and co-founder of Fipto

Three Spiko funds are available to Fipto clients. The Spiko EU T-Bills Money Market Fund (EUTBL) accepts subscriptions in euros and EURC, with a net annualised yield of 2.09% against the €STR benchmark as at the announcement date. The Spiko US T-Bills Money Market Fund (USTBL) accepts USDC balances and carries a net annualised yield of 3.37% in US dollars, benchmarked to the Federal Funds Rate. The Spiko Amundi Overnight Swap Fund, in its EUR class, is available from euro balances and yielded 2.84% net annualised on the same date, with asset management delegated to Amundi. All three funds accrue daily, including at weekends, meaning balances placed before the Friday cut-off continue earning across Saturday and Sunday.

The structural mechanics matter as much as the yield figures. Each Fipto client is onboarded directly as a Spiko investor and holds fund shares in its own name rather than through a pooled account. Fipto acts as introducer and provides the interface; Spiko Finance SAS provides the investment service. Fund assets are held in custody with CACEIS Bank. These are not bank deposits and carry no deposit guarantee protection, a point the firms disclose explicitly.

The regulatory stack is fully licensed on both sides. Fipto holds a Payment Institution licence from the ACPR and MiCA CASP authorisation from the AMF. Spiko Finance SAS is an investment firm authorised by the ACPR, and the funds are UCITS approved by the AMF.

Patrick Mollard, co-founder and chief executive of Fipto, said the combination of fast settlement and in-platform yield allocation represents where corporate finance is headed. “Money moves the moment the business needs it, and does not sit still the rest of the time. And because the rails and the allocation run through the same API, the same flow works whether a treasurer triggers it, a rule triggers it, or in time an AI agent does.”

Market context

The partnership sits at the intersection of two trends that have been reshaping institutional cash management in Europe. First, the growth of stablecoin-denominated treasury operations among mid-sized and large corporates, accelerated by MiCA’s entry into force and the clarity it provides for euro-denominated stablecoins. Second, the push by regulated asset managers and fund distributors to reach crypto-native corporates who hold meaningful working capital in stablecoins but have had no friction-free path to yield.

Several competitors are circling the same opportunity. Banking-as-a-service providers and crypto-focused neobanks have launched yield products backed by money market funds or T-bills, typically for retail or semi-institutional clients. What Fipto and Spiko are targeting is the operational treasury layer: balances that are not investable in the traditional sense because they need to remain liquid for payment runs but that sit idle for hours or days because stablecoin rails settle faster than counterparties can deploy the incoming cash.

The weekend accrual feature is commercially relevant precisely because 24/7 settlement creates a structural dead zone that traditional bank sweeps cannot address. Whether the yield rates on offer are compelling enough to move treasurers who are already comfortable with their existing bank arrangements is the open question. Redemptions return within one to two business days, which introduces a small but real liquidity gap for treasurers who need same-day access to funds. That constraint will bear watching as the product matures.

Firms crack down on money mules but need to do more

              

  

  

  
    

    

      

Financial firms are shutting down hundreds of thousands of suspected money mule accounts, but organised criminal groups are still shifting dirty money through multiple bank accounts before cashing out.

  

            						

An FCA survey found firms have closed an increasing number of suspected mule accounts over the last 3 years: 238,396 suspected mules had their accounts closed in 2025, up from 184,935 in 2023 and 233,269 in 2024.

An increase in account closures could reflect broader customer growth alongside improvements in identifying and acting on suspected mule activity, rather than necessarily meaning mules make up a higher proportion of firms’ business.

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates more than £100bn is laundered through the UK or UK corporate structures each year. Money mule activity is one way criminals move these funds, by using people’s bank accounts to receive or transfer money on their behalf.

Account closures were highest among customers aged 26 to 39 (91,073), while the sharpest increase was among customers aged 40 to 49 (37,274 in 2025 up from 25,760 in 2024). Customers aged 25 and under (85,425) also represented a significant proportion of closures.

The financial regulator also found evidence that criminals moved fraudulent funds through multiple accounts, usually cashing out between the second and fifth account. By this stage, payments are harder to detect and trace, and shows that firms need to crack down on activity as early as possible.

Some accounts had been used repeatedly for mule activity before firms shut them down and had also been used for fraud. This points to an established criminal infrastructure rather than opportunistic, isolated incidents.

The FCA, NCA, Home Office, the Treasury and industry are leading on 9 system priorities (PDF) as part of the UK’s response to economic crime. The FCA is playing a key role on the money mules priority by working with industry on an action plan to tackle the problem, including better ways for firms and law enforcement to share intelligence on suspected money mule activity.

Steve Smart, executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Money muling is a crime and it's not victimless. It makes it harder to recover stolen cash and helps criminals move and hide the proceeds of serious offending. People should be wary of contact out of the blue, including via online channels, asking them to funnel money through their account as they could face prosecution.

'It's good that financial firms are taking action on mules, but banks, law enforcement, technology companies and consumers all have a role to play in stopping people being drawn into criminal activity.'

  

Money mule warning signs to look out for

If you’re approached out of the blue online with an offer of quick cash, then alarm bells should ring.  

Scammers may call it a 'job offer' but no legitimate company will ask you to use your own bank account to transfer their money.  

Never give sensitive financial details to someone you don’t know and trust.

Be aware that the consequences of becoming a money mule could include losing access to your bank account and possible prosecution. 

Find out more about money transfer scams.

Notes to editors

Read our multi-firm review: Money mules: mule activity and cashing out findings.

Alongside the National Economic Crime Centre, the FCA is alerting firms to its latest findings.

Fighting financial crime is one of the FCA’s strategic priorities (PDF).

The FCA surveyed 35 retail banks, building societies, challenger banks, payment institutions and e-money institutions.  

The FCA also established a public/private cell in 2025 – a working group with 22 regulated firms. The cell looked at 140 cases, covering 7 types of fraud.

The FCA found card payments were the most common cash-out method and used to make lots of low-value transactions, or higher-value payments to local businesses and retailers. This can resemble legitimate consumer spending and be harder for firms to detect.    

Retail banks accounted for most transactions passing through mule accounts, whereas other firms experience lower volumes but higher-value transactions. This suggests different criminal behaviours, cash-out strategies and risk concentrations. 

The Home Office’s Fraud Strategy 2026 to 2029 recognises the role that money mule networks play in facilitating fraud and financial crime.

This work follows previous publications on detecting and preventing money mules, and firms' use of the National Fraud Database (NFD) and money mule detection tools.

title: Fed names new payments chief
snippet: Federal Reserve Financial Services tapped Kim Robbins to succeed Mark Gould starting in November.
fullText:
The Federal Reserve’s financial services division has appointed Kim Robbins as its new top payments executive, tapping her to replace the retiring Mark Gould.

Federal Reserve Financial Services announced the appointment Thursday, picking a nearly 20-year Federal Reserve veteran to lead the division that provides payments services to financial institutions. She’ll step into the role on Nov. 16, according to the press release stating her appointment.

She has served as first vice president and chief operating officer at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City since March 2024 and has been with that reserve bank in some capacity since January 2012, according to her LinkedIn profile. Prior to heading to that regional bank, she worked for Federal Reserve Financial Services as the chief of enterprise services.

In a post last week on that social media site, Robbins said she was pleased to “return ‘home’ to payments.” She also gave a nod to the work that lies ahead.

“With rapid innovation transforming the industry, it is clear to me that we are in a pivotal moment in payments,” she said. “I look forward to partnering across the Federal Reserve System and with our industry stakeholders to advance modern, secure, and resilient payment services that meet the dynamic and evolving needs of financial institutions, businesses, and the American public.”

Gould is retiring after spending the last three years with a key focus on rolling out the Fed’s instant payments system FedNow, starting in mid 2023, and trying to lure banks across the country to join the system. As of this month, the central bank has attracted just over 1,900 U.S. banks and credit unions to use the real-time payments system.

With some 8,500 financial institutions in the U.S. eligible to use the system, the Fed has a ways to go in drawing more banks and credit unions to the new service. Last month, the Fed began offering a discount program to entice financial institutions to participate in the service.

Only U.S. financial institutions can join the system, which enables them to send payments in a matter of seconds or minutes, as opposed to transactions sometimes taking days to settle. The Fed launched the instant payments system in July 2023 in the hopes of bringing smaller banks into the realm of faster payments. That followed the start of a private real-time system, the RTP Network, by bigger banks that own The Clearing House in November 2017.

In late 2024, the Fed disclosed that it cost about $246 million to operate the FedNow payments system that year, after requiring about $100 million for development in 2023, according to a report from the central bank. 

The central bank this year has also been exploring how to extend the reach of the system across international borders. Last month, the Fed said the real-time system was “on the verge” of providing cross-border transaction “support,” but then it stopped short of saying how and when. 

Robbins has leadership experience both with respect to FedNow as well as the broader Federal Reserve Financial Services, the release said. 

Specifically, the release noted that she was FedNow’s chief administrative officer, leading the “functions supporting the program’s rapid scale-up across multiple Federal Reserve Banks,” plus “strengthening the governance, risk, compliance and legal structures” for the system.

Aside from FedNow, Robbins will oversee the Fed’s retail, wholesale and securities services for financial institutions, the release noted.

Before Robbins joined the Fed, she had an early start to her career in a different kind of retail sector. She worked for seven years for the GAP and Payless ShoeSource, managing various aspects of the retail chains’ business lines.

Victims of a £1.5m crypto investment fraud will recover lost funds after the FCA obtained confiscation orders against Raymondip Bedi and Patrick Mavanga.

  

            						

At a hearing at Southwark Crown Court on 28 September 2026, Raymondip Bedi was ordered to pay £603,404.28 and Patrick Mavanga £247,997.99.

Between February 2017 and June 2019, Bedi and Mavanga operated a fraudulent investment scheme, cold-calling consumers and persuading them to invest in fake cryptoasset opportunities through companies including CCX Capital and Astaria Group LLP. At least 65 investors were defrauded and lost £1,541,799.

The FCA has identified and contacted victims of the fraud and will ensure that funds recovered through the confiscation process are returned to victims.

In July 2025, following an FCA prosecution, Raymondip Bedi was sentenced to 5 years and 4 months' imprisonment and Patrick Mavanga was sentenced to 6 years and 6 months' imprisonment for their roles in the scheme.

Steve Smart, joint executive director of enforcement and market oversight at the FCA, said:

'Bedi and Mavanga defrauded investors and left them out of pocket. These orders bring victims a step closer to getting money back.

'We’ll keep coming after fraudsters and holding them to account.'

Raymondip Bedi’s date of birth is 9 October 1989.

Patrick Mavanga’s date of birth is 24 November 1984.

FCA secures convictions against two individuals for £1.5m fraud.

Two individuals sentenced to a combined 12 years for £1.5m crypto fraud.

title: Tap Global Appoints Moorwand to Issue New Multi-Currency Mastercard
snippet: Tap Global's 400,000-user platform will offer customers direct multi-currency spending from app balances, with card interchange and FX as operating revenue. The post Tap Global Appoints Moorwand to Issue New Multi-Currency Mastercard appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Tap Global Group plc (AIM: TAP), the AIM-listed digital finance platform, has appointed Moorwand Ltd as issuer and Bank Identification Number sponsor for a new Tap Mastercard programme, extending an existing partnership that already underpins the e-money accounts in the Tap app.

The move is primarily a product upgrade. The current Tap card is euro-denominated, meaning that purchases in other currencies trigger a conversion at the point of sale. The new card is designed to let customers spend directly from whichever currency balances they hold in the app: a customer paid in sterling spends in sterling; a customer travelling in a local-currency market draws down a balance held in that currency. Tap says the multi-currency card has been its most-requested feature from its base of approximately 400,000 users.

The commercial logic

Arsen Torosian, CEO and co-founder at TAP Global PLC

The arrangement carries a direct revenue rationale. Card interchange fees and foreign-exchange margin are both operating revenue lines for the Group, alongside trading fees and what Tap calls Tap Earn income. Putting more currencies on a single card and expanding into additional markets widens the pool of transactions against which both revenue streams accrue. Tap did not disclose projected interchange volumes, FX spread assumptions or a timeline for the additional market launches.

Moorwand is an FCA-authorised Electronic Money Institution and a principal member of Mastercard, which means it can act as BIN sponsor without routing through a third-party processor for scheme access. That principal membership is commercially significant: it reduces the number of intermediaries between Tap and the Mastercard network, lowers per-transaction cost in principle and, according to Tap, gives the Group a single platform on which to develop new card features and payment use cases as it enters new markets.

Arsen Torosian, group CEO and co-Founder, said: “A multi-currency card has been the feature requested most often by our customers, and this programme delivers it. It also gives us a stronger foundation for new payment features and expansion into additional markets over time. Card interchange and FX are operating revenue, so every card we put in a customer’s hand earns for the Group.”

Market and regulatory context

The multi-currency prepaid card space is well-populated. Wise, Revolut and several other FCA-regulated e-money institutions already offer cardholders the ability to hold and spend in multiple currencies from a single account, and competition on FX spread is intense in that segment. For Tap, the differentiation proposition is integration with its crypto-adjacent digital finance app rather than a standalone prepaid product.

From a regulatory standpoint, card issuance in additional markets will require compliance with local licensing and Mastercard scheme rules on a market-by-market basis, as Tap acknowledges in its announcement. The FCA authorisation that Moorwand holds is valid in the UK and, under the post-Brexit framework, does not automatically passport into EU jurisdictions. Any European expansion will require its own regulatory pathway, either through Moorwand’s EU entity or a separate issuing arrangement. That incremental compliance overhead is worth watching as the Group’s market expansion plans become more specific.

The October 2025 e-money partnership with Moorwand provides a working foundation. Consolidating both the account and card infrastructure under a single principal partner reduces operational complexity and, in theory, should accelerate future product iteration. The near-term markers for investors and observers will be the timing of card launch for existing users, the specific additional markets targeted and any disclosure of early card-spend data.

title: Amex dinged by Fed, OCC
snippet: American Express must pay a $350 million penalty after regulators cited “significant deficiencies” in its anti-money laundering program.
fullText:
The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve Board concurrently issued enforcement actions against American Express and its subsidiaries Thursday over failures in their anti-money laundering programs.

American Express National Bank was hit with a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty by the OCC, while American Express and its travel-related services arm received a cease-and-desist from the Fed.

Amex’s bank subsidiary, based in Sandy, Utah, failed to tailor its Bank Secrecy Act/anti-money laundering risk assessment to its business activities, according to the OCC, by focusing too much on its “relatively narrow” demand deposit account products and services and not enough on the risks in its “more dominant” credit and charge card products.

Additionally, the bank experienced “systemic breakdowns” in its suspicious activity monitoring and reporting processes, resulting in roughly $13 billion of suspected trade-based money laundering activity between June 2014 and May 2025, the OCC said.

The Fed called $308 billion-asset Amex’s AML program issues “enterprise wide,” but particularly an issue at its national bank subsidiary.

“The OCC expects banks of American Express’s size and complexity to devote sufficient resources to ensure compliance with laws and regulations designed to detect and prevent money laundering, which are critical to both economic and national security,” said Comptroller of the Currency Jonathan Gould in a prepared statement.

Amex’s banking subsidiary is now required to create an action plan within 90 days to address its compliance deficiencies as well as develop an effective BSA/AML risk assessment process and consumer due diligence and risk identification program, according the OCC order, It must also engage a third-party to conduct a suspicious activity review look-back.

Under the Fed order,, Amex is required to submit a plan to improve its enterprise-wide BSA/AML compliance risk management program. TRS must submit to the Fed a plan to address Office of Foreign Assets Control compliance.

Amex “takes its responsibility to combat financial crimes seriously,” and that it will address the concerns of both the Fed and the OCC, the company’s CEO, Stephen Squeri, said Thursday in a post on the Amex website.

“Over the last few years, we have engaged closely with regulators as we have strengthened our controls and with law enforcement to provide information,” Squeri said in the statement.

“While we have made meaningful progress, we know there is more work to do,” he said.

A portion of the civil money penalty was “reserved for in prior periods,” he said, and it does not impact the full-year 2026 guidance. The consent orders are not anticipated to affect Amex’s 2027 guidance, he said.

This is the first civil money penalty imposed on a bank by the OCC since the $450 million penalty it levied against TD in October 2024, according to OCC data.

Toronto-based TD’s penalty was also related to BSA/AML issues, but amounted to much more: more than $3.5 billion in penalties overall, and a $434 billion asset cap on TD’s U.S. retail banking operations.

fullText:
The FCA and Practitioner Panel annual survey of regulated firms provides valuable insights into how firms think we’re performing.

The latest survey shows 79% of firms are highly satisfied with their relationship with the FCA, up from 74% last year. The proportion of firms rating the FCA as a highly effective regulator also increased from 69% to 76%, while 75% reported high levels of trust.

Firms were most confident in our work to protect consumers (87%), ensure markets work well (85%) and enhance the integrity of the UK financial system (85%). There was a 27-percentage point increase in firms’ understanding of the Secondary International Competitiveness and Growth Objective and a 25-percentage point increase in confidence in our delivery of it.

We took on board feedback from last year’s survey and provided further guidance to help firms embed the Consumer Duty. This year, 88% of firms say they understand what we expect on supporting consumers and embedding the Duty.

The findings also provide valuable insight into where firms would like to see further progress, including on regulatory burden. We’re already simplifying reporting by removing outdated or duplicated data returns for 90% of firms.

Nikhil Rathi, chief executive of the FCA, said: 'A year into our strategy it's encouraging to see growing confidence across many areas of our work. We know there is more to do. For example, while we can’t do our job without the data firms provide, we should continue to simplify requests and make them easier to manage.'

Matt Hammerstein, chair of the FCA Practitioner Panel, said: 'This year’s survey results indicate firms continue to have broadly positive views of the FCA, including strong understanding of expectations under the Consumer Duty and significant growth in confidence in the FCA’s ability to deliver on its secondary objectives focused on growth and competitiveness.

'The Panel is encouraging the FCA to be clearer about the outcomes it expects its priorities to produce, and more vocal about the progress it is making against these, to strengthen confidence in the UK as a leading global financial centre and attractive place to invest.'

In the first year of our strategy, we've delivered an estimated £5.6bn in benefits to consumers and the economy, including launching My FCA, reducing reporting burdens to save firms around £16m annually, and introducing nearly 50 pro-growth measures to boost UK competitiveness and innovation. 

Since the survey was conducted, we’ve continued our work to deliver landmark reforms, including working with HM Treasury and the Financial Ombudsman Service to modernise the redress framework, support industry delivery of the Advice Guidance Boundary Review, regulating Buy Now Pay Later products, establishing a new regime for cryptoassets, and progressing the PISCES private markets framework.

title: Where platforms are losing (and winning) merchants: Inside switching triggers
snippet: Merchants are willing to switch. Learn which platform factors drive loyalty and retention.
fullText:
Software providers have less room than ever to assume merchants will stay put.

For the second year in a row, more than 60% of merchants say they have an appetite for switching platforms. In 2025, that figure stood at 62%, up from 55% in 2023, according to the 2026 Merchant Insider Report, which surveyed more than 1,500 businesses across Australia, the UK and the US.

Software providers need to understand what causes businesses to reconsider their current platform and what gives them a reason to stay. 

Payment satisfaction is the #1 reason businesses are unlikely to switch software providers. 

For platforms, payments are a key indicator of whether merchants feel supported enough to stay or frustrated enough to look elsewhere. 

Where platforms lose: when “good enough” stops being enough

Switching triggers point to stagnation, friction and poor fit more than any single product gap.

Among businesses likely to switch, the report found:

32% cite newer, more innovative software options

28% say they spend too much time managing their current solution

28% want a provider better suited to their industry

27% say integrations no longer meet requirements

25% say their contract is ending

The report also found that 25% of likely switchers mention bad customer experiences using payment capabilities.

Together, these findings show how operational frustrations become switching triggers. When software takes too much time to manage, integrations fall short and payment experiences frustrate customers, the platform may no longer fit the business. 

That is where platforms begin to lose ground. Not because one feature is missing, but because the overall experience feels harder than it should.

Where platforms win: when payments strengthen loyalty

When the payment experience is reliable, easy to manage and well-integrated, it reinforces the value of the platform around it. Payments support the way merchants work. 

The platforms winning merchants are making payment capabilities feel current, useful and native to everyday workflows. That does not require chasing every headline-grabbing feature. It requires practical capabilities that help merchants accept the payment types they need, connect reliably to other systems, move money efficiently and keep pace with customer expectations.

Flexibility is becoming part of the retention equation

Another pattern emerges across the switching triggers: merchants are looking for platforms that adapt to their business, not the other way around.

Some merchants need simple payment capabilities, while others need more complex workflows, stronger integration support or additional ways to manage money movement. Those needs can shift as they grow. 

For software providers, the right payments relationship can make that flexibility easier to deliver. When payment capabilities can expand alongside merchant needs, platforms have more room to retain customers through different stages of growth.

Regional triggers show different routes to the same risk

The report revealed regional differences in platform priorities. 

In Australia, businesses are especially focused on innovation, time spent managing solutions and integration improvements. In the UK, industry fit, innovation and time spent managing the solution rise to the top. In the US, innovation, integration improvements and bad customer payment experiences stand out.

The priorities vary, but merchants are consistently measuring platforms by how well they fit their business. 

What switching triggers should tell software providers

Switching triggers are product map clues. 

If merchants are spending too much time managing their current solution, the opportunity may be to reduce manual work. If integrations no longer meet requirements, the opportunity may be to improve reliability. If innovation is driving switching consideration, the opportunity may be to make product improvements more visible. 

If customer payment experiences are disappointing, the opportunity is to make the payment journey easier and more trustworthy. 

The loyalty opportunity

Merchants are more willing to switch than they were a few years ago. But they are not unreachable. The same report that shows rising willingness to switch also shows the strongest reason they stay: satisfaction with payments.

That is the opportunity. Platforms that make payments feel reliable, flexible and valuable give merchants a clear reason to stay. Platforms that let payments become rigid, disconnected or outdated give them a reason to look elsewhere.

The switching signals are getting harder to ignore. For software providers, the path forward is not to assume merchants will stay put. It is to make staying feel like the smarter choice.

Get all the switch signals in the full report
